title: Gateless Barrier, Case 14: Nan-ch'uan Kills the Cat
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 14 of the Gateless Barrier, Nan-ch'uan kills the cat, at a Samish sesshin, first setting it beside Mary Oliver's poem "The Summer Day" and the title's "barrier that has no gate." Most of the hour reads Norman Fischer's commentary, which compares the case to Solomon and the baby, gives Dogen's alternate replies, and reads Zhaozhou's sandals on his head as mourning for a cat already dead. Norman also pictures the quarreling East Hall and West Hall monks as meditators and workers. Nomon adds Ryokan weeping over a wayward teenager, then a friend who answers a rude son with "that hurts my feelings," and the son apologizes.

In the Zen precept study, it's always noted that there are three levels of precept practice: the literal, the compassionate, and the ultimate level.
On the literal level, we follow the precepts according to their explicit meaning.
Not to kill means not to kill, not even a bug.
But on the compassionate level, we recognize the complexity of living.
Sometimes not to kill one thing is to kill something else.
And the network of causality is endlessly complex and our human ideas cannot encompass it.
We recognize that precepts will be broken sometimes on this compassionate level.

In most monasteries in ancient China, the community was divided.
Some monks lived in the meditation hall, devoting full time to formal practice.
